title: batcher-handoff-jitter-inflight-horizon-jun-2024
content:
Context and motivation:
- Running into intermittent tail-latency spikes on small-req, bursty traffic. Average token latency looks fine but P99/P999 has recurring ~40-120ms blips that correlate with increased kernel serialization in traces.
- Hypothesis: the user-side microbatcher / host work-queue is occasionally delivering tightly-packed handoffs that force the device-side kernel queue into serialization. There is visible jitter when the batcher toggles between immediate dispatch and short-deferral (to coalesce).

What I profiled / tools used:
- nsight-systems: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt -o handoff-raw --sample=cpu --cpuctx-switches true --capture-range c1:c2 to get only the window around spike samples.
- nvprof not used (deprecated) — all traces are from Nsight Systems with high-resolution CPU sampling and NVTX markers emitted from batcher and serving runtime.
- perf / top on host to rule out scheduler preemption.
- tiny Lua harness to reproduce: 200 concurrent clients, Poisson arrivals lambda=0.2, request size=16 tokens.

Quick reproduction notes (local dev machine, A100):
- start runtime with REDWOOD_TRACE_NVTX=1 and ENABLE_BATCHER_HYSTERESIS=1 (flag toggles short deferral).
- start nsys capture before load generator so timestamps align with NVTX markers.
- workload: bursty arrivals, mean interarrival ~100ms with occasional 10–20ms bursts.

Observations from traces:
- NVTX markers show these phases: host-enqueue -> batcher-coalesce-window -> dispatch-host -> cudaStreamSynchronize? -> kernel-launch.
- On spike windows I saw multiple consecutive kernel launches on the same stream separated by tiny gaps (~200–800us). These gaps are *not* the kernel duration — they are host-side serialization gaps where the next launch waits on the CPU to submit.
- CPU-side sampling shows the thread responsible for dispatch occasionally descheduled for ~1ms during high host load, causing the stream queue to accumulate ready-to-run kernels and then dump them in quick succession. This looks like a microburst on the device: several kernels queued back-to-back causing SM contention and L2 thrashing.
- The device-side timeline shows short-lived kernels (<250us) followed by a slightly longer kernel that does KV cache updates. The longer kernel suffers 2–5x slowdown when it runs after a flurry of tiny kernels (memory bandwidth hotspot).

Key metrics from run-target windows (median / spike window):
- host dispatch latency (nvtx:dispatch->submit): median 85us / spike 1.1ms
- inter-launch gap on stream: median 400us / spike 120us (i.e., tighter packing during spikes)
- average SM occupancy during packed window: dropped 25% relative to median (SM idling increases)
- L2 utilization: +34% during packed launches, followed by higher L2 miss latency for the larger kernel
- CPU core frequency stayed stable; the issue is scheduling/descheduling of the dispatch thread, not power throttling.

Root cause hypothesis (multi-factor):
1) Batcher hysteresis toggling: when hysteresis flips (coalesce vs immediate dispatch) it sometimes triggers a tight sequence of dispatch operations as it flushes queued requests.
2) Host dispatcher thread preemption: dispatch is single-threaded per-worker and pinned to a cgroup rshared core; under bursty CPU work it can be descheduled causing multiple kernels to be sent in quick succession when it resumes.
3) Device-side sensitivity: our kernels include an L2-heavy KV update phase that performs poorly when preceded by a set of small compute kernels that saturate memory pipes briefly, leading to higher-than-expected L2 miss latencies.

Experiments tried and outcomes:
- Increase batcher deferral window by +2ms: P99 reduced by ~18% but average token latency increased slightly. Good for steady burst mitigation but hurts sustained throughput.
- Move dispatcher to a dedicated high-priority thread (SCHED_FIFO) vs using niceness tweak: reduced dispatch descheduling events in traces, P999 spikes disappeared on local reproducer. However requires infra judgment for production (SCHED_FIFO and priority inversion concerns).
- Add randomized jitter to flush timings (uniform 0-200us): smoother dispatch cadence, reduces kernel packing events; P99 improved ~12% without material cost to throughput in tests.
- Channeling small kernels onto a separate stream pool to give the larger KV-update kernel a less-saturated path: mixed results due to L2 contention (same L2 cache sets across streams).

Actionable proposals (short -> medium -> long):
- Short term (patch): introduce small randomized jitter on batcher flush and a config knob BATCHER_FLUSH_JITTER_US default 50-150. Roll as feature-flagged.
- Short term: increase dispatcher thread priority / pin to a less-contended core in Dedicated/Docker deployments where safe to do so. Add runtime metric that counts dispatch-deschedule-events (increment when dispatch->submit gap > 1ms).
- Medium term: implement an adaptive coalescing policy that scales deferral with observed dispatch descheduling rate and request-size distribution.
- Medium term: split kernels by criticality: defer non-critical small kernels to a low-priority stream and reserve a small set of streams for large, memory-sensitive kernels to avoid back-to-back interference. Requires more careful testing across GPUs and multi-process setups.
- Long term: investigate kernel-level throttling / micro-sleep injection in host submissions to smooth device queueing under heavy bursty traffic. Alternatively, explore per-stream semaphore-based pacing (device-side) if supported by runtime.

Telemetry & instrumentation changes recommended:
- Emit NVTX marker pairs around dispatch critical sections with tags: dispatch_id, batch_size, flush_mode, thread_id. Already added prototype in PR linked above.
- Perf counters: track number of kernels submitted within 1ms window per stream; expose histograms in console for P50/P99 of inter-launch-gap.
- Add host metric: dispatch-deschedule-rate (count & histogram of dispatch->submit gap). Use this to trigger adaptive coalescing.

Open questions / risks:
- Will jittering flush timings adversely affect downstream SLAs for very latency-sensitive single-token requests? Need canary experiments with real customer traffic.
- Priority boosting of dispatcher threads could cause priority inversion or unfairness under noisy co-tenants in shared nodes. Must gate via config by deployment type (Dedicated vs Hosted).
- Multi-GPU colocated tenants: device L2 behavior may differ; some GPUs (older Ampere) show stronger negative interaction. Need cross-GPU matrix tests.

Next steps and owners:
- (Ava) land BATCHER_FLUSH_JITTER feature-flag + unit tests (PR draft ready). Track perf in staging for 48h with bursty workload.
- (Diego) prototype dispatcher priority worker in a side branch, validate no regressions in canary.
- (Priya) schedule cross-GPU test matrix (A100, A10G, H100 if available) to validate L2/memory interference; collect Nsight traces for each.
- (Team) add dispatch-deschedule-rate metric and dashboard tile; baseline current clusters for comparison.

Appendix: useful trace snippets and commands used
- nsys capture: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --sample=cpu --cpuctx-switches true -o /tmp/handoff-20240622.nsys --stats=true --force-overwrite --capture-range c1:c2 --processes-all
- NVTX marker naming convention (proto): 
  NVTX_PUSH: batcher:coalesce:start:size=3
  NVTX_PUSH: batcher:coalesce:end:size=3
  NVTX_PUSH: dispatcher:submit:batch_id=42
  NVTX_PUSH: kernel:kv-update:batch_id=42
- Minimal repro harness available in /dev/repro/batcher-jitter.js (internal wip)

Notes to self:
- Avoid immediate SCHED_FIFO in hosted until we have safe toggles. Use pinning + niceness in hosted for now.
- Cross-check kernel launch parameter ordering to make sure we don't accidentally serialize via cudaStreamSynchronize or explicit cudaDeviceSynchronize calls in helper libs.

If anyone else has seen similar patterns (pack of small kernels + bad performance on subsequent memory-heavy kernels) please drop trace ids here or in #eng-runtime.
